missions/apostolic-mission/name: The apostles and the Jerusalem church (30–100)
missions/apostolic-mission/statusNote: The Jerusalem community was scattered by persecution and by the Jewish revolts of 66–70 and 132–135; its Jewish-Christian form became marginal, while the movement it launched became the largely Gentile episcopal church of the second century.
missions/apostolic-mission/summary: The first Christian mission: a Jewish messianic community in Jerusalem, led by Peter, John and later James the brother of Jesus, which proclaimed the crucified Jesus as risen Messiah, spread through Judaea, Samaria and the Jewish diaspora, and — after fierce debate — accepted Gentiles without circumcision. Most of what later tradition says about the apostles' journeys beyond the Book of Acts (Thomas to India, Mark to Alexandria, Peter's death in Rome) ranges from probable to legendary.
missions/apostolic-mission/story:
The Christian mission began among the followers of Jesus of Nazareth in Jerusalem shortly after his crucifixion, usually dated c. 30 or 33. The Book of Acts, written perhaps a generation or two later, describes the Twelve, Mary the mother of Jesus and other disciples gathering in the city and, at the pilgrim feast of Pentecost, proclaiming that God had raised Jesus and poured out his Spirit. The early community was thoroughly Jewish: it worshipped in the Temple, kept the Law and understood itself as the renewed Israel of the last days. Acts portrays shared property, common meals and rapid growth; its round numbers (3,000, then 5,000) are best read as Luke's way of signalling success rather than as counts.

Tension soon arose between Aramaic-speaking ‘Hebrews’ and Greek-speaking ‘Hellenists’ over the care of widows (Acts 6). Seven Hellenist leaders were appointed, among them Stephen and Philip. Stephen's critique of the Temple led to his stoning (c. 34), and the persecution that followed — in which Saul of Tarsus took part — scattered the Hellenists. Ironically this dispersion became the engine of mission: Philip preached in Samaria and baptised an Ethiopian court official on the Gaza road; others went to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, where unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene first preached to non-Jews and the disciples were first called ‘Christians’.

Peter, according to Acts, toured the coastal plain (Lydda, Joppa) and baptised the Roman centurion Cornelius at Caesarea, a story Luke uses to legitimise the admission of Gentiles. Herod Agrippa I executed James son of Zebedee c. 44 and imprisoned Peter, after which leadership in Jerusalem passed to James the brother of Jesus. The great crisis of the movement — whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Law — was settled in principle at the meeting in Jerusalem c. 48/49 (Acts 15; Galatians 2), which accepted Paul's uncircumcised converts while asking them to observe minimal purity rules. The quarrel at Antioch, where Peter withdrew from table fellowship with Gentiles under pressure from ‘people from James’, shows how unsettled the question remained.

The Jerusalem church paid a heavy price for its position between the Jewish authorities and the Gentile mission. James was stoned on the order of the high priest Ananus in 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200). During the revolt of 66–70 the community, according to Eusebius, withdrew to Pella across the Jordan; the destruction of the Temple in 70 and the expulsion of Jews from Jerusalem after the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135) ended its leadership. Thereafter Jewish-Christian groups (later labelled Nazarenes and Ebionites) survived in Syria and Transjordan but were increasingly treated as heretical by a predominantly Gentile church.

Beyond Acts, the apostles' later careers are known almost entirely from tradition. That Peter died in Rome under Nero (c. 64–67) is early (1 Clement, Ignatius, the second-century ‘trophy’ on the Vatican hill) and widely accepted. That John lived at Ephesus is a second-century tradition (Irenaeus) still debated. Eusebius records that Mark was Peter's interpreter and founded the church of Alexandria; the claim is traditional and cannot be verified. The Acts of Thomas (early third century, Syriac) sends Thomas to the Indo-Parthian king Gondophares, whose historicity is confirmed by coins; the St Thomas Christians of Kerala hold that he landed at Muziris in 52 and was martyred near Mylapore in 72. Other apostolic legends — Andrew in Scythia, Bartholomew and Thaddeus in Armenia, James in Spain — are later still.

By about 100 the movement had communities across the eastern Mediterranean, in Rome and probably in Egypt and Mesopotamia, held together by itinerant teachers, letters and the memory of the apostles. Its lasting achievement was the decision, reached through conflict, that faith in Jesus could be lived out by people of every nation without becoming Jews — the founding principle of all later cross-cultural Christian mission.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/0: Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate, had been raised by God and exalted as Messiah and Lord.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/1: The outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost marked the beginning of the promised last days and empowered witness.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/2: Repentance and baptism in the name of Jesus brought forgiveness of sins and entry into the restored people of God.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/3: The Scriptures of Israel (in Hebrew and Greek) were read as prophecies fulfilled in Jesus.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/4: Jesus would soon return in glory, giving urgency to the proclamation.
missions/apostolic-mission/beliefs/5: Gentiles could be included in God's people; after debate, the majority view held that they need not be circumcised.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/0: Public preaching at Jewish festivals and in the Temple courts, where diaspora pilgrims could carry the message home.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/1: Synagogue-based proclamation to Jews and God-fearing Gentiles across the diaspora.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/2: House-based communities sharing meals, prayer, the ‘breaking of bread’ and (in Jerusalem) common property.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/3: Itinerant apostles, prophets and evangelists moving between cities, supported by local hospitality.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/4: Appointment of leaders (the Seven, elders) to manage growth and care for widows and the poor.
missions/apostolic-mission/strategies/5: Letters and envoys linking scattered communities to Jerusalem and to one another.
missions/apostolic-mission/groupsReached: Aramaic-speaking Jews of Jerusalem and Galilee.
Greek-speaking diaspora Jews (Hellenists) resident in or visiting Jerusalem.
God-fearers and proselytes such as the Ethiopian official and the centurion Cornelius.
Gentiles in Antioch, first reached by unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene.
Jewish communities of Egypt, Rome and Mesopotamia, by channels that are largely unrecorded.
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/0: Opposition from the Temple authorities and Herodian rulers: Stephen stoned (c. 34), James son of Zebedee executed (c. 44), James the Just stoned (62).
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/1: Bitter internal dispute over circumcision, food laws and table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/2: Poverty in the Jerusalem community, relieved by collections from Antioch and Paul's churches.
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/3: The Jewish revolts of 66–70 and 132–135, which destroyed Jerusalem and dispersed the mother church.
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/4: Roman suspicion, culminating in Nero's persecution in Rome after the fire of 64.
missions/apostolic-mission/challenges/5: The delay of Jesus' expected return, which required reinterpretation of early hopes.
missions/apostolic-mission/harms/0: Disputes between Jewish and Gentile believers produced lasting bitterness, visible in the Antioch incident and in polemical New Testament passages.
missions/apostolic-mission/harms/1: The ‘parting of the ways’ left texts (e.g. John's language about ‘the Jews’, Matthew 27:25) that later Christians read as licence for anti-Judaism and persecution.
missions/apostolic-mission/harms/2: Jewish-Christian groups faithful to the Law were gradually marginalised and condemned as heretical by the Gentile majority.
missions/apostolic-mission/harms/3: Ethnic tension between Hebrews and Hellenists over the neglect of widows showed early discrimination within the community.
missions/apostolic-mission/harms/4: Later legends of apostolic foundations were used competitively to bolster the prestige and jurisdiction of particular sees.
missions/apostolic-mission/developments/: The principle, established at the Jerusalem meeting c. 48/49, that Gentiles could join without adopting Jewish law — the basis of cross-cultural mission.
A model of community life combining worship, shared meals, teaching and care for the poor.
The first Christian leadership offices (apostles, elders, the Seven) and the practice of collective decision-making.
The preservation of oral traditions about Jesus that fed into the written Gospels.
Networks of communities from Jerusalem to Rome by the 60s, linked by envoys and letters.
Founding memories (Peter in Rome, Mark in Alexandria, Thomas in India) that shaped the identity of later churches.
missions/apostolic-mission/outcome: Within seventy years a Jewish renewal movement had become a trans-ethnic network of communities from Mesopotamia to Rome. The Jerusalem church itself did not survive as a centre of leadership, but its decision to welcome Gentiles transformed Christianity into a missionary faith open to every culture.
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/0/r: Leading apostle and spokesman of the Twelve
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/0/f: Preaching in Jerusalem and the coastal plain; baptised Cornelius; later travelled to Antioch and, by early tradition, Rome
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/0/o: Martyred in Rome under Nero according to early and widely accepted tradition
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/1/r: Leader of the Jerusalem church from the 40s
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/1/f: Law-observant leadership; brokered the compromise on Gentile converts
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/1/o: Stoned at the instigation of the high priest Ananus in 62 (Josephus)
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/2/r: Apostle; one of the ‘pillars’ of Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9)
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/2/f: Jerusalem and Samaria in Acts; second-century tradition places him at Ephesus
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/2/o: Tradition that he died old at Ephesus is ancient but debated
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/3/f: Preaching among Greek-speaking Jews; critique of the Temple
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/3/o: Stoned; regarded as the first Christian martyr
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/4/f: Samaria, the Ethiopian official, the coastal towns from Azotus to Caesarea
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/4/o: Settled at Caesarea with his prophesying daughters (Acts 21)
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/5/r: Early benefactor and envoy of the Jerusalem church to Antioch
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/5/o: Parted from Paul over John Mark and went to Cyprus
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/6/f: By tradition Parthia and India (Muziris 52, Mylapore 72)
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/6/o: Venerated as founder by the St Thomas Christians of Kerala; historicity debated
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/7/r: Companion of Barnabas, Paul and Peter; traditional author of Mark's Gospel
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/7/f: Cyprus, Rome; by tradition founder of the church of Alexandria
missions/apostolic-mission/keyPeople/7/o: Revered as first patriarch by the Coptic Church (traditional)
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/0/t: Birthplace of the mission: preaching at Pentecost, a community of several thousand by Luke's account, and the base of the Twelve and later of James.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/1/t: Philip the Evangelist preached in a city of Samaria; Peter and John followed. A first crossing of an ethnic-religious boundary.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/2/t: Believers were in Damascus by Paul's conversion (c. 34). At Antioch Hellenists first preached to Gentiles and the name ‘Christians’ arose; it became the base of the Gentile mission.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/3/t: Hellenists scattered after Stephen's death preached in Tyre, Sidon and Cyprus, at first only to Jews (Acts 11:19).
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/4/t: Acts 8 describes the baptism of a court official of the Kandake of the Kingdom of Meroë; no lasting church is recorded from this.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/5/t: Christians existed in Rome before Paul, probably among Jews expelled under Claudius (c. 49). Nero blamed them for the fire of 64; Peter and Paul died there by early tradition.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/6/t: Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew, knew of Jesus (Acts 18:24). Eusebius records that Mark founded the Alexandrian church — a tradition that cannot be verified.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/7/t: Traditional: Thomas is said to have landed at Muziris (Kodungallur) in 52 and to have been killed near Mylapore in 72. Roman trade routes made such a voyage possible; there is no contemporary evidence.
missions/apostolic-mission/countries/8/t: Beyond Paul's work, second-century tradition places John and other Palestinian disciples (Philip and his daughters at Hierapolis) in the province of Asia.
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/0/ti: Philip the Evangelist: Samaria, the Gaza road and the coast
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/0/st: Gaza road (baptism of the Ethiopian official)
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/0/te: After Stephen's death Philip preached in Samaria, baptised the Ethiopian treasurer on the desert road to Gaza, then evangelised the coastal towns from Azotus to Caesarea, where he settled (Acts 8; 21:8).
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/1/ti: Peter: Jerusalem, the coast, Antioch and (traditionally) Rome
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/1/te: Acts records Peter's journeys to Lydda, Joppa and Caesarea; Galatians places him at Antioch c. 49. His presence and martyrdom in Rome (c. 64–67) rest on early tradition (1 Clement, Ignatius, the Vatican ‘trophy’) and are widely though not universally accepted.
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/2/te: Mark accompanied Barnabas and Paul to Cyprus (Acts 13) and later Barnabas alone. Papias and Eusebius make him Peter's interpreter in Rome; Eusebius (Hist. Eccl. 2.16) says he was the first to preach in Egypt and found churches in Alexandria. Coptic tradition holds he was martyred there c. 68. The Alexandrian part of the route is traditional.
missions/apostolic-mission/journeys/3/te: Kerala tradition holds that Thomas sailed on the Roman monsoon trade route, landed at Muziris in 52, founded seven churches on the Malabar coast and was martyred at Mylapore in 72. The third-century Acts of Thomas instead sends him to King Gondophares in the north-west (Taxila region). Both are traditional; neither can be confirmed from contemporary sources.
missions/apostolic-mission/relations/0/t: Antioch, founded by scattered Hellenists and supervised by Barnabas, commissioned Paul and Barnabas for the first journey (c. 46).
missions/apostolic-mission/relations/1/t: The apostolic networks became the episcopal churches of the second and third centuries, which claimed apostolic foundation.
missions/apostolic-mission/relations/2/t: Syriac churches traced their origins to Thomas and to Addai (Thaddaeus), sent to Edessa — traditions that underpinned the Church of the East's identity.
missions/apostolic-mission/agreements/0/: At the Jerusalem meeting (c. 48/49) James, Peter and John recognised Paul's Law-free Gentile mission and asked only that he ‘remember the poor’ — the collection Paul later brought.
missions/apostolic-mission/disagreements: Some Jerusalem believers (the ‘circumcision party’) insisted Gentile converts be circumcised; at Antioch Peter and Barnabas withdrew from mixed table fellowship under pressure from James's envoys and Paul publicly rebuked Peter (Galatians 2).
missions/apostolic-mission/deviations/0: The early community of goods (Acts 2–4) was not sustained or widely imitated beyond Jerusalem.
missions/apostolic-mission/deviations/1: The movement began as a renewal within Israel but became, within a century, a largely Gentile body that distanced itself from Judaism.
missions/apostolic-mission/deviations/2: Law-observant Jewish Christianity, once the mainstream in Jerusalem, came to be treated as heterodox by the later church.
missions/apostolic-mission/deviations/3: Second- and third-century apocryphal Acts embellished the apostles' missions with miracle legends far beyond the historical evidence.
